questions.q: A share costs {p} and earnings per share are {e}. What's the P/E ratio?
You'll receive {c} in {n} years. You could earn {r} a year elsewhere. What's it worth today?
A company's market cap is £{m}m, it has £{d}m of debt and £{c}m of cash. What's its enterprise value, in £m?
questions.why: EV = market cap + debt − cash = £{answer}m: the price of the whole business.

questions.q: If interest rates rise, the present value of a company's future profits usually rises.
questions.why: Higher rates mean a higher discount rate, so future cash is worth less today. That's why share prices often fall when rates rise.

questions.q: A share has a P/E of 5 while similar companies are on 15. What's the most sensible conclusion?
options: Find out why: the market may expect its profits to fall
The P/E will rise to 15 next year
questions.why: A low P/E can be a bargain or a value trap. Ask why it's cheap before buying.

questions.q: Put the steps of a DCF valuation in order.
items: Forecast free cash flow for the next few years
Estimate a terminal value for the years after
Add it up and divide by the number of shares
questions.why: Forecast, add a terminal value, discount, then sum and divide by shares.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: The yearly return you require for waiting and risk
A DCF's value for all years after the forecast
questions.why: These are the building blocks of how analysts value companies.

questions.q: What does a high P/E ratio usually suggest?
options: Investors expect strong profit growth or see the company as safe
The company is about to go bust
The share price is definitely too high
The company pays a big dividend
questions.why: Investors pay more per £ of today's profit when they expect more profit later or see little risk.

questions.q: A DCF valuation gives a precise, reliable value that doesn't depend much on your assumptions.
questions.why: Small changes to growth or the discount rate can move the value by 10% or more. Treat it as a range.

questions.q: Explain why £100 in five years is worth less than £100 today.

ideas.label: Money today could be invested to earn a return (opportunity cost)
Waiting has risk and inflation shrinks what it buys

questions.model: £100 today could be invested and grow to more than £100 in five years, so future money must be discounted to compare fairly. Waiting also carries risk (you might not get paid) and inflation shrinks what it can buy.

tests.answer: Because you could invest the £100 today and earn interest, and there's risk and inflation while you wait.
Because you could earn interest on it now.

questions.q: Explain why a DCF valuation can change a lot with small changes in assumptions.

ideas.label: Most of the value is in the distant future (the terminal value)
So small changes to growth or the discount rate compound over many years

questions.model: Most of a company's value usually comes from the terminal value, the cash far in the future. Small changes to the growth rate or discount rate compound over all those years, so they swing the total a lot.

tests.answer: Most of the value comes from the terminal value far in the future, so a small change in the discount rate compounds over many years.
Because it depends on the discount rate.
Because share prices change every day.
